It is recommended that you keep notes about what you are investigating and what you find as this will make the process of creating your presentation and report easier. Please note that you _do not_ need to submit this file as part of your group project.



```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```


```{r load-lib, message = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
# Add any other libraries here
```

```{r load-data}
# load your data 
crime_data <- read.csv(
  "data/communities.data",
  header = FALSE,
  na.strings = "?",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

name_lines <- readLines("data/communities.names")
attribute_lines <- grep("@attribute", name_lines, value = TRUE)

variable_names <- sub("@attribute ", "", attribute_lines)
variable_names <- sub(" .*", "", variable_names)

length(variable_names)

colnames(crime_data) <- variable_names
```

```{r}
## Stage1.1  Dataset Structure
# Overall dimensions
dim(crime_data)

# Number of observations
nrow(crime_data)

# Number of variables
ncol(crime_data)

# Names of all variables
names(crime_data)

# Types of variables
variable_types <- table(sapply(crime_data, class))

knitr::kable(
  as.data.frame(variable_types),
  col.names = c("Variable Type", "Number of Variables"),
  caption = "Types of Variables in the Dataset"
)

#  Preview of the first six observations
knitr::kable(
  head(crime_data[, 1:10]),
  caption = "First Six Observations (First Ten Variables)"
)
```

```{r}
## Stage1.2 Investigate missing values
# Total number of missing values
sum(is.na(crime_data))

# Number of missing values in each variable
missing_values <- colSums(is.na(crime_data))

missing_table <- data.frame(
  Variable = names(missing_values),
  MissingValues = as.numeric(missing_values)
)

knitr::kable(
  missing_table,
  caption = "Missing Values in Each Variable"
)
```
```{r}
## Stage1.3 select relevant variables
crime_selected <- crime_data %>%
  select(
    communityname,
    ViolentCrimesPerPop,
    PctPopUnderPov,
    medIncome,
    PctUnemployed,
    PctBSorMore,
    PctVacMore6Mos
  )

colnames(crime_selected) <- c(
  "Community",
  "ViolentCrime",
  "Poverty",
  "MedianHouseholdIncome",
  "Unemployment",
  "Education",
  "LongTermVacancy"
)

dim(crime_selected)
str(crime_selected)

head(crime_selected)

missing_summary <- data.frame(
  Variable = names(crime_selected),
  MissingValues = colSums(is.na(crime_selected)),
  MissingPercentage = round(
    colMeans(is.na(crime_selected)) * 100, 2
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  missing_summary,
  caption = "Missing Values in Selected Variables"
)

sum(is.na(crime_selected))
summary(crime_selected)
```
```{r}
## Stage1.4 Data Visualisation

library(tidyverse)

# Distribution of violent crime rates
ggplot(data = crime_selected,
       mapping = aes(x = ViolentCrime)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of violent crime rates",
    x = "Normalised violent crime rate",
    y = "Number of communities"
  )

```
this histogram shows a positively skewed distribution of normalised violent crime rates. Most communities have relatively low crime rate values, with the highest concentration occurring around 0.05. The frequency decreases as crime values increase. There are also some observations with particularly high crime values near 1. This suggests that there is variation in violent crime rates across communities, which we aim to investigate using socioeconomic variables.



```{r,message=FALSE}
ggplot(data = crime_selected,
       aes(x = Education, y = ViolentCrime)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Education and Violent Crime",
    x = "Educational Attainment",
    y = "Violent Crime Rate"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
## Stage3.1  Descriptive Statistics
eda_data <- crime_selected %>%
  select(-Community)

descriptive_stats <- data.frame(
  Variable = names(eda_data),
  Mean = round(sapply(eda_data, mean), 3),
  Median = round(sapply(eda_data, median), 3),
  SD = round(sapply(eda_data, sd), 3),
  Minimum = round(sapply(eda_data, min), 3),
  Maximum = round(sapply(eda_data, max), 3)
)

descriptive_stats
```

```{r}
## Stage 3.2 Correlation Analysis
cor_matrix <- cor(
  eda_data,
  use = "pairwise.complete.obs",
  method = "pearson"
)

round(cor_matrix, 2)

```
```{r}
## Stage 3.3 Correlation Heatmap

cor_data <- as.data.frame(as.table(cor_matrix))

ggplot(cor_data,
       aes(x = Var1, y = Var2, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(Freq, 2)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "blue",
    mid = "white",
    high = "red",
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-1, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Correlation Heatmap",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Correlation"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```
Poverty (r = 0.52) and unemployment (r = 0.50) have the strongest positive correlations with violent crime, suggesting that communities with higher levels of poverty and unemployment tend to have higher crime rates. On the other hand, median household income (r = -0.42) and education (r = -0.31) have negative correlations, meaning that communities with higher incomes and education levels generally have lower crime rates. Long-term housing vacancy (r = 0.02) shows almost no correlation with violent crime.

We also found that some socioeconomic factors are strongly related to each other. For example, poverty is negatively correlated with income (r = -0.79) but positively correlated with unemployment (r = 0.78). This could lead to multicollinearity when we carry out regression analysis, as some variables may be explaining similar patterns in the data.
```{r}
## Stage 3.4 Correlation bar chart 

# Extract correlations with violent crime
crime_correlations <- cor_matrix["ViolentCrime", ]

# Remove violent crime's correlation with itself
crime_correlations <- crime_correlations[
  names(crime_correlations) != "ViolentCrime"
]

# Convert into a data frame
cor_df <- data.frame(
  Variable = names(crime_correlations),
  Correlation = as.numeric(crime_correlations)
)

# Create bar chart
ggplot(cor_df,
       aes(x = reorder(Variable, -Correlation),
           y = Correlation)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#F28DBB", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", Correlation)),
    vjust = ifelse(cor_df$Correlation >= 0, -0.5, 1.5),
    size = 4
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey40") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.6, 0.65)) +
  labs(
    title = "Correlation with Violent Crime",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Pearson Correlation Coefficient"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```
